1408.title: Punjab's shared devotional ground
1408.hook: a street is closed with a tent, a lamp is lit, and nobody plans to sleep
1408.howItsDone: Punjabi Hindu families hold a jagran, or jagrata, for Mata, for instance in thanks for a blessing: singers lead devotional songs through the night before a lit jyot, and prasad is shared at dawn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punjab's shared devotional ground: Ravidas at his bench, and the Ganga in a cobbler's bowl.

Nine at night in a Punjabi neighborhood. A lane is closed off with a bright tent. On a stage draped in red and gold sits a picture of the Goddess on her lion, a lamp burning in front of her. Plastic chairs fill up, then the floor: aunties, kids in pajamas, uncles who said they'd stay an hour. A singer with a harmonium starts, and the whole tent answers back: Jai Mata Di. Victory to the Mother. Nobody here plans to sleep. Today, the night a Punjabi family stays awake for the Goddess.
screen: `A LANE TURNED INTO A TENT.` → `A LAMP BEFORE THE GODDESS.` → `JAI MATA DI.`

segments.voice: It's called a jagran, or in Punjabi, a jagrata: a waking, a vigil. Why hold one? It can be a thank-you. A child was born, a son or daughter married, a new house finished, an illness passed, a prayer answered. So the family invites the Goddess, Durga, called simply Mata, Mother, and keeps her company through the night. The lamp in front of her, the jyot, isn't allowed to go out. All night, singers lead bhents, songs offered to the Mother in Punjabi and Hindi, fast and slow, some about the hill shrines where her devotees climb to see her. Those shrines sit in the mountains north of the Punjab plains: Vaishno Devi in a cave, Jwalamukhi where flames burn out of the rock, Chintpurni, Naina Devi. A jagran brings a little of that mountain into a city lane. People dance. Kids fall asleep on laps and wake up for the loud parts. Tradition keeps a story for the last hours, the tale of a devoted queen named Tara, told as the night turns gray. And the point is in the name. Staying awake for someone is what love does: a parent with a sick child, a friend at a hospital bed. A jagran turns that love toward the Mother; the family that was cared for stays up to keep her company. The whole lane is invited. At dawn there's prasad, sweet food blessed and shared, and everyone goes home tired, and full.
screen: `JAGRAN — A WAKING, A VIGIL` · `A THANK-YOU TO THE MOTHER` · `SONGS ALL NIGHT, THE LAMP KEPT LIT` · `STAYING AWAKE IS WHAT LOVE DOES`

segments.voice: Let your breath call and answer like the tent: the in-breath calls, the out-breath answers. Then think of someone who once stayed awake for you, or someone you stayed awake for, and let them be here in the quiet; if you pray, let the answer be the tent's words, Jai Mata Di, and keep the Mother company.

1409.title: Punjab's shared devotional ground
1409.hook: a winter bonfire, a fistful of sesame and popcorn, and a song about an outlaw
1409.howItsDone: On Lohri night, Punjabi families and neighbors light a bonfire, walk around it tossing in sesame, peanuts, rewri and popcorn, and celebrate a new baby's or new bride's first Lohri with special warmth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punjab's shared devotional ground: the jagran, a night awake for the Mother, with the whole lane invited.

Cold enough to see your breath. A courtyard in Punjab, and in the middle, a bonfire taller than the kids around it. Someone presses a handful into your palm: sesame seeds, peanuts, a little hard sweet called rewri, a few pieces of popcorn. Everyone walks around the fire and throws a pinch in. The flames jump. Earlier, children went door to door singing, and came home with sweets and coins. The song is about an outlaw. Today, Lohri. Back on day one hundred fifty-two it got one line; today it gets the whole fire.
screen: `A BONFIRE IN THE COLD.` → `SESAME AND POPCORN IN THE PALM.` → `A SONG ABOUT AN OUTLAW.`

segments.voice: Lohri comes in the deep of winter, on the night before Maghi, the day tradition counts as the start of the sun's northward journey. First, the fire. For Hindus, a fire receiving offerings is old ground. In the Vedic rituals, offerings are poured into Agni, the fire, who carries them up to the gods. At Lohri there's no priest and no chanting required, just a family throwing sesame and grain into the flames. But the shape is familiar: give something to the fire, and the fire carries it on. Some families bow to the fire as they go around it. Then, the people. Lohri belongs to the Punjabi year itself, so Hindus, Sikhs and their neighbors keep it, each in their own way. It's especially loud for a family with a first: a new baby's first Lohri, a new bride's first Lohri in her husband's home. The bonfire becomes a welcome. Then, the song. The children's door-to-door song is about Dulla Bhatti, a Punjabi Muslim folk hero remembered as an outlaw who, the story says, rescued a poor girl and saw her married as if she were his own daughter. So on a winter night, around a Hindu household's fire, kids sing about a Muslim outlaw with a good heart. That's the ground Punjab shares. Each family brings its own prayers to the fire, and the same heat reaches every face around it.
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE MAGHI` · `AN OFFERING INTO THE FIRE` · `A WELCOME FOR EACH NEW FIRST` · `A SONG FOR DULLA BHATTI`

segments.voice: Cup one hand in your lap as if it holds sesame and popcorn, and think of one thing from this season you'd gladly give to the fire: a worry, a grudge, a tiredness carried too long. Hold it for a few breaths, then open the hand on an out-breath; if you pray, offer it to God, or to Agni, as the fire does.

1410.title: Punjab's shared devotional ground
1410.hook: the wheat turns gold, and one spring day means different things to the neighbors who keep it
1410.howItsDone: Hindus in Punjab keep Vaisakhi as the harvest and the solar new year, some bathing in a sacred river or temple tank at dawn, visiting the temple and giving to others; harvest fairs fill the villages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punjab's shared devotional ground: Lohri, a winter fire, sesame in the flames, and a song for Dulla Bhatti.

Months after the Lohri fire, the fields have changed color. The wheat planted in the cold stands gold and heavy, and the sickles are coming out. In the villages there's a fair: drums, swings, sugarcane, bangles on a blanket, young men dancing bhangra with their arms up as if lifting the whole harvest. The day is Vaisakhi. Walk through the crowd asking what the day means, and you'd hear more than one answer. Today, one spring day that Punjab's neighbors share, each keeping it in its own way.
screen: `THE WHEAT TURNS GOLD.` → `DRUMS, SWINGS, BHANGRA.` → `MORE THAN ONE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Vaisakhi takes its name from the month of Vaishakh, in the spring. First, the harvest. For farming families in Punjab, it's when the year's work pays off: months of watching the sky and worrying about rain, and now the grain is ready. Thanks comes before the cutting. Then, the Hindu year. For Hindus in Punjab, Vaisakhi is also a new year by the solar calendar, the day the sun enters a new sign, so a day for new beginnings. Some families bathe in a sacred river or a temple tank at dawn. Some visit the temple, offer the first of the grain, and give to those who have less. A new year starts with a clean body, a full granary and an open hand. Then, the neighbor's meaning. For Sikhs, Vaisakhi remembers the day Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa, kept with processions, prayer and service. That meaning belongs to the Sikh tradition, and Sikhs tell it in their own words. A Hindu family and a Sikh family on the same street can both keep Vaisakhi, side by side, neither one borrowing the other's story. And at the fair, all of them hear the same drums. So shared ground doesn't mean everyone believes the same thing. It means the same day, the same fields, the same harvest, and neighbors who know what the day means to each other.

segments.voice: Think back over the past season and let one thing come to mind that you planted and that has quietly grown: a skill, a friendship, a habit, a patience you didn't have before. Hold it the way a farmer holds the first sheaf, with thanks and without boasting; if you pray, offer that first sheaf to God.

1411.title: Punjab's shared devotional ground
1411.hook: a queen left alone at the forest's edge, and the poet who finds her
1411.howItsDone: Pilgrims visit Ram Tirath near Amritsar, honored in tradition as Valmiki's hermitage, and Valmiki's birthday is kept in Punjab with processions and devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punjab's shared devotional ground: Vaisakhi, one spring day, each neighbor keeping its own meaning.
screen: `THE SAME DAY, EACH ITS OWN MEANING.`

segments.voice: A woman sits alone at the edge of a forest, crying. She is Sita, the queen of Ayodhya, and she's carrying a child. Ram has sent her away because of what people in the city were saying, and the brother who drove her here has gone back. Young students from a nearby hermitage hear her and run to tell their teacher. He comes out to her. He's Valmiki, the poet of the Ramayana, and he finds the heroine of his own story weeping at his door. Today, Punjab's last stop: a place tradition calls that door.
screen: `SITA ALONE AT THE FOREST'S EDGE.` → `THE STUDENTS RUN FOR THEIR TEACHER.` → `VALMIKI COMES OUT.`

segments.voice: In the last book of Valmiki's Ramayana, in paraphrase, Valmiki speaks gently to Sita. He tells her he knows she has done no wrong. He brings her into his hermitage and gives her into the care of the women there, to be looked after like a daughter. First, the shelter. The poet who tells the whole story of Ram also shelters Sita when the story turns hard on her. Her twin sons, Lava and Kusha, are born there and grow up in the hermitage. Valmiki teaches them the Ramayana, and in the story they sing it, their own father's story, before Ram himself. Then, the place. Tradition places Valmiki's hermitage at Ram Tirath, near Amritsar. There's a temple and a sacred tank, and pilgrims come to the place where, the story says, Sita found shelter and her sons were born. Last, who honors him. Tradition calls Valmiki the first poet, the adi kavi. In Punjab, the Valmiki community honors him with special devotion as Bhagwan Valmiki, and his birthday is kept with processions. Each comes to him in its own way, and the place holds them all. And that's where the regional journey ends: Tamil hymns, Bengal's streams, the Varkari road, Kashmir, Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa, Gujarat's courtyard of questions, and Punjab, where songs, festivals and holy places are held as shared ground. Tomorrow, before the festivals that close the year, the path stops and sits at the top of the climb.
screen: `VALMIKI SHELTERS SITA` · `THE TWINS LEARN THE RAMAYANA` · `RAM TIRATH, NEAR AMRITSAR` · `HONORED BY EACH IN ITS OWN WAY`

1412.title: the summit sit
1412.hook: a king without a kingdom and a merchant without a family sit in a forest and ask a sage the same question
1412.howItsDone: Some devotees of the goddess recite the Devi Mahatmya in full, in one sitting or spread across the nights of Navaratri.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punjab's shared devotional ground ended at Ram Tirath. Today the climbing stops for a while.
screen: `PUNJAB'S SHARED DEVOTIONAL GROUND.` · `THE CLIMBING STOPS FOR A WHILE.`

segments.voice: A forest hermitage. A king sits on the ground; his ministers turned on him and his enemies took his city. Beside him sits a merchant whose own wife and sons threw him out for his money. The strange part: the king keeps worrying about his old elephants and his treasury. The merchant keeps wondering whether his family is well. Both know these thoughts make no sense. So they ask the sage: why can't the mind let go? That's where this year began. Today's summit sit goes back to that forest.
screen: `A KING WITHOUT A KINGDOM.` → `A MERCHANT WITHOUT A FAMILY.` → `WHY CAN'T THE MIND LET GO?`

segments.voice: A summit sit is a stop near the top of the year. The path has climbed a long way: the goddess, Shiva, the schools, the Vedas, the epics' women, the regions. Now each day looks back at one part of the climb and sits with it. Start with the Devi Mahatmya. The king is Suratha, the merchant Samadhi, the sage Medhas, and his answer is the whole book. The pull they feel, he says, is the goddess as Mahamaya, the great power that draws the minds of even the wise into confusion. Then he tells them who she is, through her stories: the goddess leaving the sleeping Vishnu so that he wakes to face two demons; the goddess given every god's weapon to face the buffalo demon Mahisha; the goddess who meets Shumbha and Nishumbha, with Kali springing from her brow. The same power that binds the mind, Medhas says, sets it free. The book ends not on a battlefield but by a river. They worship the goddess there, and she appears and asks what each wants. The king asks for his kingdom back, and she grants it. The merchant asks for the knowledge that loosens the grip of me and mine. She grants that too. Same question, two different answers. And the question is an ordinary one: why does my mind keep going back to what hurt me? The book doesn't scold it. It builds a whole scripture around it.
screen: `A SUMMIT SIT: ONE STRETCH, SEEN FROM THE TOP.` · `THE KING, THE MERCHANT AND THE SAGE.` · `THE POWER THAT BINDS IS THE POWER THAT FREES.` · `A KINGDOM BACK, OR A LOOSENED GRIP.` · then, large: `THE QUESTION IS NOT SCOLDED.`

If a hurt is too heavy to hold alone, please reach out: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

1413.title: the summit sit
1413.hook: is a snake lying still a different snake from the one that moves?
1413.howItsDone: Shakta devotees worship the goddess as the power that moves the world, reciting hymns such as the Saundarya Lahari and the Lalita Sahasranama, and calling her simply Mother.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit went back to the Devi Mahatmya, and the king's question: why can't the mind let go?
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `WHY CAN'T THE MIND LET GO?`

segments.voice: Is a snake lying coiled in the sun a different snake from the one that slides off into the grass? Nobody would say so. Same snake, resting, then moving. That small picture is credited to Sri Ramakrishna, the temple priest of Dakshineswar, and the year used it to open a whole stretch of teaching. In the weeks after the Devi Mahatmya, the path stopped telling the goddess's stories for a while and asked what she is. Today's summit sit climbs back to that question: Shakti, as a way of thinking.
screen: `A SNAKE, COILED.` → `THE SAME SNAKE, MOVING.` → `WHAT IS THE GODDESS?`

segments.voice: Shakti means power: the power to act, to make, to move. In the teaching remembered from Ramakrishna, when the divine is thought of as still, beyond all doing, he called it Brahman. When it is thought of as creating, keeping and dissolving the world, he called it Shakti, the Mother. Not two things: one snake, at rest and in motion. Now take that picture to a hymn the year read. The Saundarya Lahari, a long poem to the goddess traditionally credited to Shankara, opens with a startling sentence. In paraphrase: Shiva, joined with Shakti, is able to create; without her, the god cannot so much as stir. A hymn of praise that starts by saying the great god can't move a finger on his own. That's the Shakta turn: power isn't a tool that someone holds. Power is the goddess herself. From up here, look how often the year came back to it. The goddess rising out of the gods' own blazing power in the Devi Mahatmya, every weapon handed over to her. The Rig Veda hymn where a goddess speaks for herself: I move with the gods, I bend the bow. The Lalita hymn that names the goddess as Shiva and Shakti in one form. Different texts, one thread: the world is not dead matter waiting for a spirit. It moves, and the moving is divine. Shakta teachers, and the Shaiva teachers beside them, read that thread in different ways and argue about how the two are related. But the thread is there to argue about.
screen: `SHAKTI: POWER, THE POWER TO MOVE.` · `STILL, BRAHMAN. MOVING, THE MOTHER.` · `WITHOUT HER, SHIVA CANNOT STIR.` · `THE MOVING IS DIVINE.` · then, large: `ONE SNAKE.`

segments.voice: Let the body settle until it's mostly still, then notice what is still moving: the breath, the pulse in your hands, small shifts of balance. Don't stop any of it; let stillness and movement sit in one body, like the coiled snake and the moving snake, and if you pray, rest in the goddess as that movement.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: Shakti as a philosophy, and a snake that is the same snake, still or moving. Today's word.

1414.title: the summit sit
1414.hook: a bronze dancer in a glass case, one foot planted, one foot lifted, and everything in between meaning something
1414.howItsDone: Nataraja is worshiped in temples and homes, notably at Chidambaram in Tamil Nadu, and the figure is honored in classical dance, where dancers often begin by saluting him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit looked back at Shakti, and a snake that is one snake, coiled or moving.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `ONE SNAKE, STILL OR MOVING.`

segments.voice: A glass case in a quiet gallery. Inside, a bronze figure stands in a ring of flames. One foot is planted. The other is lifted and swung across. Hair flies out to the sides as if the figure just spun. People walk past with their phones out and walk on. But on this path, a whole week went into standing in front of that figure and reading it, one hand at a time. Today the summit sit goes back to Shiva as Nataraja, the lord of the dance, and reads him all at once.
screen: `A BRONZE IN A RING OF FIRE.` → `ONE FOOT DOWN, ONE FOOT LIFTED.` → `READ IT ALL AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Back in the Nataraja week, each day took one piece. Now put the pieces back together. In one hand, a small drum; in the tradition, its beat is the sound of things beginning. In the hand across from it, a flame: the ending, held level with the beginning, neither one higher. Another hand is raised, palm out, in the gesture that says do not fear. Another arm swings across the body like an elephant's trunk, and its hand doesn't grab; it points down, toward the lifted foot. Under the planted foot lies a small figure on his belly, kept there but never finished off. Caught in the streaming hair is a tiny figure with folded hands: the river Ganga, slowed and held. Tamil Shaiva teaching reads the whole figure as the god's work in the world: making, keeping, ending, concealing, and grace. Here's what's easy to miss while you study one hand at a time. None of it happens one after another. The drum doesn't wait for the flame. The ending is already in the room while the beginning sounds. The fear-not hand is raised in the middle of the fire. The figure is one moment, with everything in it. That's worth carrying down from the summit. A week, a year, a life doesn't arrive in neat chapters; beginnings and endings share one body. This week did too: the last of the regions, Punjab's shared ground, ended just as the summit sits began.
screen: `THE DRUM AND THE FLAME, LEVEL.` · `FEAR NOT, IN THE MIDDLE OF THE FIRE.` · `THE HAND THAT POINTS TO THE FOOT.` · `EVERYTHING IN ONE MOMENT.` · then, large: `BEGINNINGS AND ENDINGS SHARE A BODY.`

segments.voice: Notice that each breath is already ending as it begins, the in-breath turning, the out-breath turning. Then let the week come to mind all at once, not in order: something that began, something that ended, something you feared, standing together like the drum and the flame held level; if you pray, rest before Shiva, the dancer, with all of it.
